---
title: "Reproducing the thesis"
subtitle: "What was confirmed, what changed, and what could not be reproduced"
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
source("R/_site_helpers.R")
```

The original analysis was done in Stata. The do-files ran from temporary directories and
did not survive; what remained was the final dataset, screenshots of output, and a
workbook recording the results. Everything here was rebuilt in R from that dataset.

The thesis does not state the specification for any of its tests — not which variant of
the Dickey-Fuller regression, not how many lags, not which deterministic terms. Each had
to be recovered by searching candidate specifications against the reported numbers. All
of them turned out to be recoverable.

## What reproduced

```{r}
#| label: tbl-repro
#| tbl-cap: "Reproduction of every statistic the thesis reports."
tibble(
  test = c("Augmented Dickey-Fuller", "Engle-Granger", "Johansen trace",
           "Granger causality", "Breusch-Godfrey", "Breusch-Pagan"),
  reported = c(66, 11, 8, 77, 11, 11),
  reproduced = c(66, 11, 6, 77, 11, 11),
  `specification recovered` = c(
    "trend in levels; constant, lag 0 in differences",
    "residual test with a constant; lags 0, 1 and 3",
    "unrestricted trend; lag order 3, Ontario 4",
    "single lag in levels with a trend, F test",
    "order 9, chi-squared",
    "against fitted values, one degree of freedom")
)
```

**179 of 181 reported statistics reproduce**, almost all to within the rounding of the
thesis's own tables. That is a strong result: the arithmetic is sound.

Two Johansen trace statistics could not be reproduced under any specification searched —
New Brunswick (reported 12.04, nearest 32.15) and Prince Edward Island (reported 16.48,
nearest 15.27). The New Brunswick figure is recorded in the source workbook against the
wrong critical value, which suggests a transcription slip. Neither changes a conclusion.

## What the re-examination changed

### The causality tests are not what they claim

The thesis describes the Toda-Yamamoto procedure, which adds extra lags to a model and
tests only the original ones. That extra padding is the entire point: it is what keeps the
test valid when the underlying series are non-stationary, as all of these are.

What actually produces the reported p-values is a single-lag regression with no
augmentation at all. The safeguard is missing.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ty
#| tbl-cap: "Causality results significant at 5%, before and after proper augmentation."
read_result("causality_vs_thesis.csv") |>
  summarise(`as reported` = sum(sig_reported),
            `Toda-Yamamoto, k=1` = sum(sig_ty_k1, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Toda-Yamamoto, k=2` = sum(sig_ty_k2, na.rm = TRUE),
            `conclusions changed (k=1)` = sum(sig_reported != sig_ty_k1),
            `of total tests` = n())
```

The headline claim survives: emissions predict output nowhere, under every specification.
The secondary findings largely do not.

### "Full rank" means the opposite of what the thesis takes it to mean

For Canada, Saskatchewan and Newfoundland and Labrador, the trace test rejects at every
rank. The thesis reads this as the strongest form of cointegration — the variables being
"fully correlated."

In this framework a rank equal to the number of variables means the system is *stationary*,
so there is nothing to cointegrate. Full rank is the absence of a cointegrating
relationship, not an abundance of one. And Canada returns it at every lag order tested, so
it is not a small-sample artifact.

The consequence is that **the Johansen test does not support the thesis's national
finding.** That finding rests on Engle-Granger alone.

### The autocorrelation problem is probably an artifact

The thesis runs Breusch-Godfrey at order 9, finds autocorrelation in three provinces, and
concludes the model "would be misspecified." But at order 9 the auxiliary regression
carries 14 regressors on 23 observations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bg
#| fig-cap: "Breusch-Godfrey p-values. British Columbia rejects at order 9 and nowhere else."
read_result("diagnostics.csv") |>
  select(geo, `1` = bg_p_order1, `2` = bg_p_order2, `3` = bg_p_order3,
         `4` = bg_p_order4, `9` = bg_p) |>
  pivot_longer(-geo, names_to = "order", values_to = "p") |>
  mutate(order = factor(as.integer(order)), grp = highlight(geo),
         bc = geo == "British Columbia") |>
  ggplot(aes(order, p, group = geo)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(aes(colour = bc, linewidth = bc), alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = PALETTE[["oil"]])) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 0.4, `TRUE` = 1.2)) +
  labs(x = "Breusch-Godfrey lag order", y = "p-value",
       caption = paste("Dashed line: 5%. British Columbia highlighted.",
                       "Genuine serial correlation shows at low orders\nand fades;",
                       "this does the reverse.")) +
  theme_site()
```

Rejections at 5% by order: **1, 0, 0, 1 — and then 3 at order 9.** British Columbia
rejects hardest at order 9 (p = 0.028) but sits at 0.66, 0.75, 0.88 and 0.24 at the lower
orders. That is not what serial correlation looks like. The misspecification the thesis
worries about may not be there.

### A result that was computed and never reported

The Breusch-Pagan heteroskedasticity results exist in the author's workbook but appear
nowhere in the document. **No jurisdiction shows heteroskedasticity at the 10% level**,
under either the Stata version or Koenker's. It is a clean result that supports the
specification, and it should have been in the thesis.

## Two things the data say that the thesis does not

**Canada is the sum of its parts.** The source workbook records that the national GDP and
emissions series were built by adding the provinces up, not taken from a separately
published national series. Checking confirms it. For a study about aggregation this
matters: the national series is an accounting identity over the provincial ones.

**Emissions do not come from Statistics Canada.** The thesis says all three series do.
GDP and energy use do; emissions come from Environment and Climate Change Canada's
official inventory.
